objective: Investigate the mini-kv store in samples/mini-kv: how does it store entries and how does TTL expiry work?

expected_claims.claim: Entries are stored in a single in-memory Map keyed by string, holding value plus an absolute expiry deadline
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the Map declaration and the Entry shape (expiresAt as Date.now()-based deadline or null)

expected_claims.claim: Expiry is lazy: it is checked when a key is read, not by any background timer
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing isExpired being called from get() and the absence of setInterval/setTimeout in the target

expected_claims.claim: Nothing is persisted; all state is lost when the process exits
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence covering the whole target surface (single source file) with no fs/serialization calls

forbidden_claims: Entries are persisted to disk or a database
Expired entries are removed by a background timer or interval
The store evicts least-recently-used entries when it grows
The store is a Redis client or uses Redis
notes: Baseline architecture case; mini-kv already exists and REA is verified on it.

objective: Investigate mini-kv's read operations (get/has) for edge cases: are there inputs or states where a read behaves surprisingly or has side effects?

expected_claims.claim: has() is implemented on top of get(), so a key explicitly set to the value undefined reports as absent
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing has() delegating to get() and comparing against undefined

expected_claims.claim: Calling has() or get() on an expired key deletes that key, so a read operation mutates the store
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the delete call on the expired branch of get()

expected_claims.claim: sweep() exists as the eager counterpart that removes all expired entries and returns how many were removed
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing sweep() iterating entries and returning a removal count

forbidden_claims: has() checks key existence directly in the Map without reading the value
Reads are side-effect free
An expired key is still returned until sweep() runs

expected_measurements.name: expiry-behavior-probe
expected_measurements.protocol: Probe program against the target: set key with ttlMs=50, wait, call get(); set key to undefined, call has(); record outcomes
expected_measurements.expectation: Expired key reads as undefined after the TTL; has() is false for a key set to undefined

notes: Quirk-detection case: full credit only if the has/get side effect is found, not just the architecture.

objective: Investigate the token-bucket-limiter: how is the rate enforced, and does the effective rate match the configured rate?

expected_claims.claim: Each key gets its own bucket stored in a Map; refill is computed lazily from elapsed wall-clock time when allow() is called, with no timers
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the per-key bucket structure and the elapsed-time refill inside allow()

expected_claims.claim: Refill credits only whole tokens (fractional accrual is discarded), so the effective long-run rate is below the configured rate when checks are frequent
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the floor/truncation in the refill arithmetic

forbidden_claims: A timer or interval refills the buckets periodically
Different keys can have different configured rates
The effective rate equals the configured rate exactly

expected_measurements.name: sustained-rate
expected_measurements.protocol: Experiment harness with a simulated or short real clock: capacity C, rate R tokens/sec; call allow() at 10x the token period for 10 simulated seconds; count allowed
expected_measurements.expectation: Allowed count matches whole-token arithmetic and is strictly below the ideal real-valued R*10+C for frequent checks

notes: Target TO BUILD per README Family A-P1.

expected_claims.claim: emit is synchronous and returns the number of handlers invoked
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing emit's synchronous dispatch and count return

expected_claims.claim: A throwing handler aborts the dispatch: later handlers for that emit do not run and the error reaches the caller
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing handler invocation without per-handler try/catch isolation

forbidden_claims: Handler errors are caught and isolated so other handlers still run
emit is asynchronous or queued
Wildcards match across multiple topic segments (like a glob **)

expected_measurements.protocol: Experiment harness: register 10, 100, 1000 matching subscribers; measure emit latency, >=30 repetitions each, same runner as src/experiments

objective: Investigate the retry-queue: how are retries scheduled, and is the maximum delay really a maximum?

expected_claims.claim: Retry delay is base * 2^attempt capped at maxDelay, plus jitter, and jobs exhausting maxAttempts land in a dead-letter list held in memory
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the delay formula and the dead-letter move

expected_claims.claim: Jitter is added after the cap, so the real delay can exceed maxDelay by up to one base unit
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the order of operations: cap applied before jitter is added

forbidden_claims: The delay never exceeds maxDelay
Failed jobs are persisted and survive a restart
A central scheduler loop drives all retries (there is one timer per job)

expected_measurements.name: delay-distribution
expected_measurements.protocol: Force a job to fail repeatedly with small base/maxDelay; record actual delays for attempts at the cap over >=30 runs
expected_measurements.expectation: Observed maximum delay exceeds maxDelay (by up to base), confirming jitter is post-cap; median grows exponentially until the cap region

objective: Investigate the session-store: sessions have sliding expiration and an absolute lifetime cap — verify both are actually enforced.

expected_claims.claim: Expiration slides: touch() extends a session's expiry by the TTL from the touch moment
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing touch() recomputing expiresAt from now

expected_claims.claim: The absolute lifetime cap is only checked at creation and never in touch(), so an actively touched session can outlive the cap indefinitely
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the cap constant/check in create and its absence from touch()

forbidden_claims: Sessions are guaranteed to end at createdAt + maxLifetimeMs no matter what
Expired sessions are removed by a background sweeper (expiry is checked on read)

expected_measurements.name: cap-survival-probe
expected_measurements.protocol: Simulated clock: create session, touch periodically past createdAt + maxLifetimeMs, then get()
expected_measurements.expectation: Session is still returned after the absolute cap has passed, as long as touches kept it unexpired

notes: Target TO BUILD per README Family A-P6. Trap case: the cap LOOKS implemented (named constant) — shallow reports will claim it is enforced.

objective: Investigate the lru-cache package source (src via the ./raw export): what bounds a cache, how does eviction work, and what happens on eviction?

expected_claims.claim: The cache supports TTL expiry with options such as allowStale and updateAgeOnGet changing read behavior for aged entries
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing TTL-related options in the source or API docs

forbidden_claims: The cache persists entries to disk
Eviction is FIFO (insertion order) regardless of reads
Keys must be strings (object keys are supported by identity)

objective: Investigate the p-queue package: what limits when tasks run, and what guarantees does the queue give about failed or waiting tasks?

expected_claims.claim: Task execution is governed by independent mechanisms: a concurrency limit, an interval/intervalCap rate limit, and per-task priority
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence from dist typings or README API showing concurrency, intervalCap/interval, and priority options

expected_claims.claim: The queue is an event emitter exposing lifecycle events such as active, completed, error, idle, and rateLimit
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the event names in typings or docs

expected_claims.claim: Tasks are held in memory only: nothing persists across a restart, and failed tasks are not retried automatically
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence covering the package surface (dist only, no storage code) consistent with the docs

forbidden_claims: Tasks are persisted to disk or Redis and survive restarts
Failed tasks are automatically retried with backoff
The queue distributes work across processes or machines

objective: Investigate lowdb: where does data live, when is it persisted, and how does the storage layer work?

expected_claims.claim: The core (Low/LowSync) is storage-agnostic: it holds data in a plain object (db.data) and delegates all I/O to a pluggable adapter with read/write methods
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the adapter interface and db.data in the source or docs

expected_claims.claim: Mutating db.data persists nothing until write() is called explicitly
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing write() as the only path from db.data to the adapter

expected_claims.claim: The bundled JSON file adapter writes atomically through the steno dependency (temp file + rename) rather than overwriting in place
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the JSONFile adapter's use of steno, or the package dependency on steno plus the adapter wiring

expected_claims.claim: Reading a database whose file does not exist leaves db.data as null; defaults are the caller's responsibility
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence from docs or source showing the null-on-missing-file behavior

forbidden_claims: lowdb is a wrapper around SQLite
Every mutation of db.data is saved automatically
Queries are executed in SQL or via an index

objective: Investigate nanoid: how are IDs generated, what makes them safe, and is the symbol distribution actually uniform?

expected_claims.claim: Default IDs are 21 symbols drawn from a 64-character URL-safe alphabet, giving about 126 bits of randomness
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the default size and alphabet in the source or README

expected_claims.claim: The default generator uses a cryptographically strong random source, not Math.random, and maps bytes to symbols without modulo bias
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the crypto source import and the bias-avoiding mapping (mask/step algorithm) in the source

expected_claims.claim: A separate non-secure variant exists that trades the strong random source for speed
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing the non-secure entry point in the package exports or docs

forbidden_claims: The default generator uses Math.random
IDs are time-ordered / sortable like UUIDv7
The library guarantees zero collisions

expected_measurements.name: symbol-uniformity
expected_measurements.protocol: Generate >=200k IDs with the default generator; chi-square test of symbol frequencies against uniform over the 64-symbol alphabet
expected_measurements.expectation: No significant deviation from uniform at alpha=0.01 (the property the README claims and upstream tests); a reconstruction or variant using naive modulo mapping must FAIL this same probe

notes: npm pack nanoid@6.0.2 (11 files, no tests in tarball). The measurement is a first-class expected claim here — this is the replica-fidelity anchor target.

objective: Using better-sqlite3's documented semantics as the reference, investigate a small fixture notes database built with it: which of the library's guarantees shape how the fixture behaves?

expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence from the fixture code or library docs showing the synchronous call style (no promises/callbacks)

expected_claims.claim: Transactions can be expressed as a function that runs inside BEGIN/COMMIT and rolls back if it throws
expected_claims.evidence_required: Evidence showing db.transaction usage or its documented semantics

expected_claims.claim: WAL mode is off unless explicitly enabled with the journal_mode pragma, and enabling it carries a checkpoint-starvation caveat under perpetual concurrent reads

WAL mode is enabled by default

objective: Investigate the semver package: how does it parse versions and decide whether a version satisfies a range?

forbidden_claims: Prerelease versions satisfy ordinary ranges by default
